title: Angry at God
hookLine: Job and the Psalms show anger can be prayer
tomorrow: Val says she'll never forgive Nico. does she have to?

lines: ALLOWED TO BE ANGRY AT GOD?
cards: A cupboard door slammed harder than it needed to be. A text typed in all caps, then deleted. Some news lands and the anger has nowhere to go.
And if you grew up praying, there's a second worry under the first one: am I even allowed to be angry at God? The Bible answers with its own prayers. Yes.
You can yell at God and still be praying.

teach.b: Job loses his children, his wealth and his health, and sits down in the ashes. Then he opens his mouth, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Let the day perish wherein I was born."

Later: "I will speak in the bitterness of my soul." His friends rush in with neat answers that defend God. At the end, God speaks, and tells the friends they have not spoken rightly about him, the way his servant Job has.

teach.h: GOD BACKS THE ONE WHO ARGUED.
teach.b: The one who argued is the one God backs. The psalms do the same thing.
"How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me unto the end?" Complaint is written right into the prayer book, and Catholics pray those psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: when Jesus cries from the cross, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" he's praying the opening of a psalm.
The anger in all these prayers is said to God, not muttered about him behind his back. It keeps talking.
That's why he can take it.

how: Catholics pray the psalms, laments included, in the Liturgy of the Hours and at Mass, and the Church reads the Passion, with Jesus's cry from the cross, on Palm Sunday and Good Friday.

o: bringing your rage to God, as prayer
losing your faith after something awful
blaming God so you don't have to grieve

games.q: anger as prayer — tap the pairs.
p: let the day perish wherein I was born

s: "the patience of Job" means Job never complained
Job curses the day he was born and argues with God at length.
in the end, God sides with Job's friends, who defended him
God says the friends did not speak rightly about him, as Job did.
Jesus on the cross prays the opening of a psalm
my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me: the start of Psalm 21 in the Douay, 22 in many Bibles.

games.q: a friend's mom just lost her job. a relative tells her, "don't be mad at God, it's disrespectful." what do the psalms suggest instead?
o: bring the anger to God in words, the way the psalms do.
swallow it and give thanks, so the anger can't grow.
stop praying until the anger passes on its own.
games.why: the psalms pray how long and why, and God backs Job over his tidy friends. anger said to God is still prayer. he can take it.

practice: Say one honest sentence out loud, quietly, the one you've been holding back: how long, or why, or this isn't fair. Don't soften it.
If you pray, say it to God, the way Job did, then sit in the quiet that follows and let it be heard.

wordCard.voice: Angry at God. The anger people hide, prayed out loud by Job, by the psalms, and from the cross.

orig.note: Latin, Psalm 12:1 in the Vulgate: how long, O Lord? the psalm's complaint in the Church's old Latin.

carryVoice: Carry this: he can take it, the way he took Job's bitterness and the psalm's how long. Good night.
